news.title: Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think
news.summary: Meta's Muse is apparently an effective AI assistant, but one that's a little creepy. Part of that is because of its new Mac app, which can access Messages, Calendar, and Notes. But for all its smarts, Muse doesn't actually know how to describe itself. Jason Aten, a contributing editor at Inc Magazine, posted on Threads […]

spec.title: Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think

claims.text: Meta’s Muse can access Messages, Calendar, and Notes through its new Mac app.
Muse said it saw notification previews rather than reading message history.
evidence_terms: I haven’t been reading your texts

claims.text: Meta said Muse syncs Messages only after the user specifically enables access.
Meta described Muse’s explanation as incorrect and said it was working to improve the assistant’s understanding of its internals.
evidence_terms: working to improve Muse’s understanding of its own internals

scenes: Slow push-in on an abstract desktop assistant interface as animated labels for Messages, Calendar, and Notes appear one by one; overlay the title “Access can feel intrusive.”
Cut to a split-screen graphic showing a notification preview beside a permission toggle changing from off to on; add the caption “What did it actually see?”
Slow pullback from a clean animated system diagram with arrows between Muse, Messages, and device sync; the arrows briefly scramble, then display “Can’t explain its own plumbing.”
spec.script: When you hear that Meta’s Muse can access Messages, Calendar, and Notes, the creepy part seems obvious. But the bigger problem may be confusion. In one reported exchange, Muse said it saw notification previews. Meta later said Muse syncs Messages only after you enable access, and called the answer incorrect. So the unsettling takeaway is an assistant that cannot reliably explain how it works.
